title: I built an AI trading agent that actually trades on its own. Now I'm trying to figure out if people would trust it with their money.
author: Much-Section-7680
selftext:
A while ago I shared a project here where I was experimenting with autonomous AI trading agents.

The idea was simple: instead of building another trading bot with fixed indicators and calling it "AI", I wanted to see what happens when you give an LLM an actual trading strategy, market data, memory, and the ability to execute trades.

I've been working on it quite a bit since then.

The interesting part isn't really getting an AI to place a trade. That's surprisingly easy.

It's getting it to behave like a disciplined trader over time.

My agents can:

* Independently analyze markets and decide which data, indicators and timeframes to look at
* Remember previous decisions and market observations
* Monitor open positions and adjust risk management
* Decide when to check the market again instead of blindly running every few minutes
* Execute trades through connected exchanges
* Explain what they're watching, why they're bullish/bearish, and what would change their mind

I'm currently running an agent live, with actual trades and performance visible publicly.

And I'm deliberately keeping that transparent. No screenshots of hypothetical 500% returns or cherry-picked backtests.

The bigger question I'm exploring now is whether this could become something people would actually use rather than just an interesting engineering experiment.

Because in theory, having an agent monitor markets 24/7, follow a defined strategy, and never get emotional sounds pretty compelling.

But obviously that doesn't automatically translate into profitability.

So I'm curious: Would you actually let an AI agent trade your account if you could define its strategy, set strict risk limits, and monitor every decision it makes?

Or would you only trust AI for analysis and keep execution manual?

For anyone interested, the project is called SoulQuant: [https://soulquant.ai](https://soulquant.ai)

Would genuinely appreciate feedback, especially from people already running automated strategies.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: I’d allow execution only if the agent’s memory is inspectable as state, not just readable explanations. Since SoulQuant lets the LLM choose indicators, timeframes, and when to check again, each decision record should preserve the exact market inputs, memory retrieved, next-wakeup condition, and risk configuration that produced it. The BTCUSDT chart visibly marks states such as WATCHING, PROMOTED, and CLOSED, but can a user replay one transition and reproduce the same action? That would make the 24/7 discipline claim much easier to trust than a narrative log alone.

replies.author: Much-Section-7680
replies.body: Good point! You can ask the agent follow-up questions about its decisions, like "Why did you take this trade?" or "What was your reasoning?" So you're not just looking at static logs, you can interact directly with the agent to understand its decisions.

comments.author: Saito53
comments.body: I did somethig similar but I made it run a simulation for the first week, gave him fake money to play with and see if he would make profit or not... It made profit, thought I kept safe with small amounts

replies.author: Technical-Athlete-9
replies.body: Sounds interesting. What evals are you doing for this agent?

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Showing live trades publicly instead of cherry-picked backtests is a good start. I'd only let an agent trade real money if the limits sit outside the model (max size, daily loss, allowed markets) and it has months of live results with fees and drawdown shown, not just wins. I'd also start with a small amount, since an LLM can decide differently on the same data. Cymetica lets you connect your own AI agent and starts it in paper mode first, which is a similar way to build trust before going live.

comments.author: tradematesHQ
comments.body: Execution is fine, blind trust isn't. If the memory and risk config aren't inspectable state, it's just a black box with a nice explain button, and those blow up quietly.

replies.author: Technical-Athlete-9
replies.body: This sounds like an LLM wrote it 3x over. Maybe commenter will trade my account.

comments.author: Naive_Refrigerator_4
comments.body: Hi. I will visit the link you posted - am so interested, as I've been looking for 100% automation.

comments.author: Technical-Athlete-9
comments.body: Most of what I see here would be better done deterministically. Other things (remember…) are not needed or could be harmful.

comments.author: CrownCreator
comments.body: For me, the step from automated strategy to agent may be a bit too much. Backtesting, running live mock and optimizing a strategy to run independently is much easier to trust than an agent adapting to the market and ‘thinking’ through what to do… I’m sure I’ll end up there eventually 😂
